memory_candidates.content: For a bash lint/script that must test whether a captured multi-line literal block of text is contained verbatim inside a target file, do NOT use `grep -F` in any form, including `grep -Fqz`. `grep -F` ALWAYS splits a multi-line PATTERN argument into one alternative pattern PER LINE and reports a match if ANY single line matches ANYWHERE in the target (an OR of single lines) -- the `-z` flag only changes how the INPUT is split into records (NUL vs newline), never how a multi-line PATTERN argument itself is split. This is a silent, easy-to-miss defect: a synthetic fixture test can pass by coincidence (if the fixture's lines happen to be unique to that fixture) while the real corpus produces false positives the moment the block contains generic recurring lines (code-fence markers, bare `{`/`}`, common boilerplate). The correct approach is bash's own native string test: `content="$(cat file)"; pattern="$(cat block_file)"; if [[ "$content" == *"$pattern"* ]]; then ...` -- quoting the variable expansion inside the glob pattern disables glob interpretation, so this performs a true literal (not glob, not regex) substring containment test, and newlines inside both operands are ordinary characters to bash's comparison. Always verify a new multi-line-containment check against the REAL target corpus, not only a synthetic fixture, before trusting it.

When collapsing N copies of 'the same' restated markdown block across N files into one-line anchor pointers, do not assume the N files' removed text is byte-identical -- real-world copies commonly carry small per-file variation (a different identifier string, a different padding/format convention, an extra sentence) baked into otherwise-shared boilerplate. A regression-lint registry for such a collapse should register ONE ROW PER FILE (each with its own captured exact removed-text snapshot), not one row per conceptual block shared across a file list, or the registry will silently fail to detect regression in files whose exact text differs from a single shared capture. Separately: a regression lint guarding a tranched (file-by-file) collapse must scope its check to only the files ALREADY collapsed and registered, never scan the whole corpus for every file still carrying the block verbatim -- the overwhelming majority of a block's sharing files are legitimately not-yet-migrated at any point mid-tranche, and a whole-corpus scan fires on all of them from the moment the first file is collapsed.

A deliverable file under a source-store tree that gets deployed/distributed (e.g. agent-system/extensions/**) must never hardcode a path into an ephemeral, per-task directory (specs/{NNN}_{SLUG}/**): task numbers get renumbered/archived during vault operations, so such a hardcoded path silently breaks later. When a task's own ephemeral inventory/analysis file is the natural DATA SOURCE for a standing lint or gate, create a separate PERMANENT registry inside the deliverable tree, seeded from (derived from) the ephemeral file at task-authoring time, rather than having the lint read the ephemeral path directly at runtime. The permanent registry is what the lint consumes forever after; the ephemeral file is just this task's one-time derivation record.
